results.question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
results.text: No. When a creature phases in, it does not trigger enters-the-battlefield abilities. The phasing event is not an enter-the-battlefield event. Rule [702.26d] explicitly states that zone-change triggers—which include enters-the-battlefield abilities (see [603.6a])—do not trigger when a permanent phases in or out. Additionally, the game does not treat the phasing event as having caused the permanent to enter the battlefield.

results.question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
results.text: Yes, the combination changes how much damage is considered lethal. When an attacking creature has both trample and deathtouch, its controller assigns combat damage by applying two rules together: deathtouch says that any nonzero amount of damage assigned to a creature is lethal (rule 702.2c), and trample says that after all blockers have been assigned lethal damage, any remaining damage can be assigned to the defending player or the planeswalker/battle the creature is attacking (rule 702.19b). So the controller must assign at least 1 damage to each blocking creature (since 1 is nonzero and thus lethal with deathtouch), and then all the rest of the creature's power can be assigned directly to the defending player or attacked planeswalker. This interaction lets even a small creature with trample and deathtouch push most of its damage through. The rules also note that for effects that check excess damage (like some replacement effects), any damage greater than 1 from a deathtouch source is excess (rule 120.4a).

results.question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
results.text: Yes, storm is a triggered ability. It functions on the stack (rule 702.40a). Triggered abilities on the stack can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities, though not by effects that only counter spells (rule 113.9). Therefore, storm can be countered, but only by something that says it counters an ability (like a Stifle effect).

results.question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
results.text: No, you cannot include a card with a hybrid mana symbol in a Commander deck unless your commander's color identity includes all colors in that hybrid symbol. A hybrid mana symbol like {R/G} is both red and green; a card featuring it has a color identity of red and green. If your commander is only red, that card's green component is outside the commander's color identity and the card is illegal.

results.question: can I respond to the untap step?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to the untap step. No player receives priority during the untap step, so spells cannot be cast, abilities cannot be activated, and no player can take actions. Any ability that triggers during the untap step is held until a player would receive priority, which happens during the upkeep step.

results.question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
results.text: Yes, creatures are still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step. The definition of an attacking creature states it remains an attacking creature until it's removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first (see Attacking Creature; 506.3c). The combat phase does not end until the end of combat step itself ends (511.3), and effects that last "until end of combat" expire at the end of the combat phase, not at the start of the end of combat step (500.5a). Therefore, throughout the end of combat step, before the step ends, attacking creatures have not yet been removed from combat and the combat phase is still ongoing, so they retain their status as attacking creatures. This applies regardless of the number of players, as the rules provided do not distinguish based on player count.

results.question: Do you cast lands?
results.text: No, you do not cast lands. Lands are played, not cast. Playing a land is a special action that puts the land directly onto the battlefield; it never uses the stack and is never a spell, so it cannot be countered. Even objects that are both a land and another card type (like an artifact land) can only be played as a land and cannot be cast as a spell. Lands have no mana cost and are played without paying any costs.

results.question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
results.text: The provided rules (702.74a) define Evoke's triggered ability as "When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it." This is a normal triggered ability, and in a complete game it would go on the stack and could be responded to before it resolves, allowing you to sacrifice the creature via another spell or ability. However, the rules context given does not include the fundamental rules governing the stack, priority, or the timing of when players can cast spells or activate abilities in response to a triggered ability (e.g., rule 117.1). Without those rules, it is impossible to conclude from the provided text alone whether you can legally take any action before the evoke trigger resolves.

results.question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
results.text: Yes, losing all abilities includes keyword abilities. Keyword abilities are a subset of abilities (rule 702.1), so an effect that says an object "loses all abilities" removes every ability that object has, including any keyword abilities. When an effect removes abilities, it removes all instances of each ability (rule 113.10b). Keywords like flying, trample, hexproof, and their variants are all abilities for this purpose. For keywords that encompass several sub-abilities (e.g., hexproof and "hexproof from [quality]", banding and "bands with other"), losing one variant typically causes the object to lose all related versions (rules 702.11e, 702.22b), so they are all stripped away. Note that losing abilities does not affect characteristics set by static abilities that are not keyword abilities, like an Aura saying "enchanted creature is red" or "enchanted creature can't be blocked" (rule 113.12).

results.question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
results.text: Yes, you can draw cards even if you're already at your maximum hand size. There is no rule that prevents drawing cards solely because your hand size is at its maximum. The maximum hand size (normally seven) only matters during your cleanup step: if you have more cards than that, you must discard down to that number. Drawing cards while at maximum hand size simply means you'll have to discard the excess later.

results.question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
results.text: When a planeswalker has 0 loyalty counters, its loyalty is 0, and it is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action. This happens automatically the next time a player would receive priority, without using the stack. The rules do not contemplate a planeswalker having less than 0 loyalty counters because counters cannot be negative; if damage would remove more counters than the planeswalker has, it simply ends up with 0 counters and then the state-based action applies.

results.question: do non-creature artifacts die?
results.text: No, non-creature artifacts do not die. The term "dies" is defined as "is put into a graveyard from the battlefield" and applies only to creatures and planeswalkers. A non-creature artifact is neither a creature nor a planeswalker, so it cannot die, even if it goes to the graveyard from the battlefield.

results.question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
results.text: If you should draw a card when your library is empty, you attempt to draw but no card moves to your hand. The next time a player would receive priority, state-based actions are checked and you lose the game. This is because a player who attempts to draw from an empty library loses that way (rule 121.4, 704.5b). If you are required to draw more than one card and have fewer than that left, you draw as many as possible, then lose at the next state-based check (rule 104.3c). If an effect replaces the card draw, that replacement is applied even if no cards could be drawn (rules 121.6a, 614.11), so you might not lose if the draw is completely replaced.

results.question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
results.text:
The combat phase has five steps, in order: beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat. If no attackers are declared, the declare blockers and combat damage steps are skipped; if any creature has first strike or double strike, there are two combat damage steps (see [506.1]). As the defending player, you gain priority at specific times in these steps based on the provided rules:

- In the end of combat step, there are no turn-based actions, and the active player gets priority first. Once the active player passes, you as the defending player get priority (see [511.1]).
- In the beginning of combat step, the provided shortcut example [732.2b] indicates that a nonactive player can have priority during that step, which normally happens after the active player passes.
- For the declare attackers, declare blockers, and combat damage steps, the provided rules do not explicitly state when the defending player receives priority. In general, under the priority system [117.1], after each step's turn-based actions (e.g., declaring attackers or blockers, assigning combat damage), the active player gets priority, then the defending player gets priority once the active player passes, but this sequence is not directly stated in the given rules.

In a multiplayer game using the Attack Multiple Players Option, all opponents become defending players [802.2], and combat damage is assigned in APNAP order [802.5], but the overall priority timing is similar.

results.question: can i respond to a mana ability?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to a mana ability. Activated mana abilities (rule 605.3b) and triggered mana abilities (rule 605.4a) do not use the stack; they resolve immediately after being activated or triggered, so they cannot be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to. This is a special exception to the normal rules for abilities (rule 405.6c).

results.question: can I respond to a cost being paid?
results.text: The provided rules do not contain a rule that explicitly states whether a player can respond to a cost being paid. While some rules suggest that paying a cost is part of another action (like casting a spell or declaring attackers) and that those actions may or may not use the stack, there is no direct statement that paying a cost itself can or cannot be responded to. A crucial rule (such as 'Paying a cost doesn't use the stack' or the steps of casting a spell from rule 601.2) is missing from the context.

results.question: can you explain layers?
results.text: Yes. The layer system (rule 613) is how Magic determines the order in which continuous effects modify an object’s characteristics. Effects are applied in a fixed sequence of layers, each handling a different type of change. Within a layer or sublayer, effects are usually applied in timestamp order (rule 613.7), but a dependency can override that (rule 613.8). The game recomputes characteristics instantly and continuously (rule 613.5). The provided rules describe these layers: layer 1 handles copiable values (rule 613.1a); layer 3 handles text-changing effects (rule 613.1c); layer 4 handles type-changing effects (rule 613.1d); layer 5 handles color-changing effects (rule 613.1e); and layer 7 handles power and toughness, with its own sublayers (rule 613.4). A practical example: Honor of the Pure gives white creatures +1/+1. If a creature turns white from an effect in layer 5, Honor of the Pure’s boost applies later in layer 7c, making it 3/3. If the creature’s color is later changed to red (layer 5 again), the boost stops applying, and it reverts to 2/2 (rule 613.5). This shows how different layers interact to produce consistent results regardless of when effects entered the battlefield.

results.question: how does the legend rule work?
results.text: Yes. The legend rule is a state-based action. If a player controls two or more legendary permanents with the exact same name, that player chooses one of them and puts the rest into their owners’ graveyards (rule 704.5j). This applies to any permanent with the legendary supertype (rule 205.4d), including planeswalkers, which now all have the legendary supertype in the Oracle card reference (rule 306.4). The rule cares only about the permanents’ names, not their card types or other characteristics. For example, a legendary token created with a specific name (see rule 111.9) is treated like any other legendary permanent. The legend rule does not affect legendary instant or sorcery spells on the stack; those are subject to a casting restriction instead (rule 205.4e), not to this state-based action.

results.question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
results.text:
Your creature dies as a state-based action the next time state-based actions are checked, which is immediately after the damage is dealt and before any player receives priority.

Damage marked on a creature doesn't destroy it directly; instead, the game rules check for lethal damage (damage greater than or equal to its toughness) as a state-based action (rule 704.5g). State-based actions are performed automatically whenever a player would get priority, and they happen before that player actually gets priority (rules 117.5, 117.2d). So after a spell like Lightning Bolt resolves and deals 3 damage to a 2/2 creature, or after combat damage is dealt simultaneously, the game checks state-based actions and destroys the creature right then—no player can respond in between the damage being marked and the creature dying. The damage remains marked until the cleanup step, but the destruction happens at the first state-based action check after the damage is applied (rule 120.6).

results.question: can I cast my commander from exile?
results.text: No, by default you cannot cast your commander from exile. A player can only begin to cast a spell if a rule or effect allows it (rule 601.3f). Commander does not grant any intrinsic permission to cast a commander from exile. The only special zone a commander may be cast from is the command zone, as specified in rule 903.8 (with the additional commander tax). However, when a commander is in exile, a state-based action allows its owner to move it to the command zone (rules 903.9a and 704.6d). So while you cannot cast the commander directly from exile, you can return it to the command zone during the next state-based action check and then cast it from there.

results.question: what happens during the cleanup step?
results.text: The cleanup step is the second step of the ending phase. During a normal cleanup step, two turn-based actions happen in order, neither using the stack. First, if the active player's hand size exceeds their maximum hand size (usually seven), they discard down to that number [514.1, 703.4n]. Second, simultaneously, all damage marked on permanents is removed and all "until end of turn" and "this turn" effects end [514.2, 703.4p]. Normally, no player receives priority during the cleanup step, so no spells or abilities can be cast or activated [514.3]. However, if after those actions any state-based actions would be performed or any triggered abilities are waiting to be put onto the stack (including those that trigger "at the beginning of the next cleanup step"), those state-based actions are performed, those triggered abilities are put on the stack, and then the active player gets priority. Players may cast spells and activate abilities. Once the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, another cleanup step begins [514.3a, 704.3]. Additionally, if an effect ends the turn during the cleanup step, a new cleanup step begins [724.1d]. If no state-based actions or triggered abilities occur, the step ends without any player receiving priority [500.3, 514.3a].

results.question: when are state-based actions checked?
results.text: State-based actions are checked whenever a player would receive priority, and also during the cleanup step. Specifically, each time a player would get priority, the game first performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously, then repeats this process until no state-based actions are performed and no triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack; only then does the player actually receive priority [704.3][117.5]. This same check-and-repeat process occurs during the cleanup step, but if the first check finds no state-based actions to perform and no triggered abilities waiting, no player gets priority and the step ends [514.3a]. Additionally, certain effects like Mandate of Peace explicitly instruct the game to check state-based actions without giving any player priority [724.2c]. State-based actions are not checked during the resolution of a spell or ability [704.4].

results.question: when can I concede a game?
results.text:
You can concede the game at any time. There is no restriction on when you may concede—it can be during your turn, an opponent's turn, in the middle of a spell or ability resolving, or even while you are controlled by another player. Conceding does not use the stack and takes effect immediately: you leave the game and lose the game right away.

This is stated directly in rule 104.3a, which says "A player can concede the game at any time." Rule 723.6 reinforces that even if another player controls your turn, you may still concede at any time. Rule 405.6g clarifies that conceding doesn't use the stack, and rule 101.1 notes that the ability to concede at any time is the one exception to the principle that card text overrides the rules.

In a Two-Headed Giant game, if you concede, your entire team leaves the game immediately and loses (rule 810.8b). In other multiplayer variants, the normal rules apply, and your concession causes you to lose and leave the game immediately.

results.question: how do I know who the active player is?
results.text: The active player is the player whose turn it is. This is defined in rule 102.1: "The active player is the player whose turn it is. The other players are nonactive players." In a game using the shared team turns option, the team whose turn it is is the active team, and the players on that team are on the active team, but the active player is still the player whose individual turn it is (if a specific player is designated as taking the turn, though the team option may alter that). See rule 805.4a.

results.question: when someone other than the active player casts a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: The player who cast the spell—the non-active player—gets priority first. Rule 117.3c states that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward. Since the non-active player had priority to cast the spell, they regain priority immediately after casting it. The active player does not automatically get priority after a spell is cast; they only receive priority after a spell resolves (rule 117.3b).

results.question: when the active player cast a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: The active player receives priority first after casting a spell. Rule 117.3c states that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward. Since the active player had priority to cast the spell, they get priority immediately after the spell is cast.

results.question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
results.text: Yes, you can hold priority to cast more spells after you've cast one. After you cast a spell, you receive priority again, so you may immediately cast another spell without passing priority to other players. This is often called "holding priority." The rule is that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward ([117.3c], [601.2i]). You can repeat this to cast multiple spells in succession before anyone else gets a chance to respond. Note that in practice, you must explicitly indicate you are retaining priority; otherwise, it's generally assumed you pass priority after casting a spell, but the rules themselves permit you to keep priority and cast more spells.

results.question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
results.text: Lore counters are put on Sagas in two distinct ways. First, as a replacement effect when the Saga enters the battlefield: a Saga without read ahead enters with one lore counter (rule 714.3a), while a Saga with read ahead enters with a number of lore counters chosen by its controller between one and its final chapter number (rules 714.3b, 702.155b). Second, as a turn-based action at the beginning of its controller's precombat main phase, that player puts one lore counter on each Saga they control that has one or more chapter abilities (rules 703.4f, 714.3c, 505.4). This turn-based action happens immediately after the precombat main phase begins (after the archenemy's scheme action in an Archenemy game) and does not use the stack.

results.question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
results.text: A delayed triggered ability is an ability created by an effect that does something later in the game rather than immediately. It contains the word "when," "whenever," or "at" (though that word usually doesn't begin the ability). A delayed triggered ability triggers only once—the next time its trigger event occurs—unless it has a stated duration, such as "this turn." It is created during the resolution of a spell or ability, as the result of a replacement effect, or as a result of a static ability that allows a player to take an action. If its trigger event occurred before the delayed triggered ability was actually created, the ability won't trigger (except for reflexive triggered abilities, which are checked immediately after creation). The source and controller of a delayed triggered ability are determined by the effect that created it (e.g., the spell, the source of the activated/triggered ability, or the object with the static ability).

results.question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
results.text: Yes, non-permanent spells (instants and sorceries) can have abilities. Rule 113.3a defines spell abilities as the abilities followed while an instant or sorcery spell resolves, and states that any text on such a spell is a spell ability unless it's an activated, triggered, or static ability that fits rule 113.6. Rule 113.6 further clarifies that abilities of an instant or sorcery spell usually function only while that object is on the stack. Therefore, non-permanent spells possess abilities, primarily spell abilities, while they are on the stack.

results.question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
results.text: Yes, you can activate a mana ability while a spell with split second is on the stack. Split second explicitly allows players to activate mana abilities even though it normally prevents casting other spells or activating non-mana abilities. Rule 702.61a defines split second as meaning "As long as this spell is on the stack, players can't cast other spells or activate abilities that aren't mana abilities," and rule 702.61b further clarifies that players may activate mana abilities and take special actions while a spell with split second is on the stack. Mana abilities themselves don't use the stack and can be activated at times when you normally couldn't take other actions (see rule 605.3a).

results.question: [Counterspell] is on top of the stack targeting my [Divination]. When everyone passes priority, what resolves first, and does Divination still resolve?
results.text:
Counterspell resolves first. Divination is countered and does not resolve; it is put into its owner's graveyard.

When all players pass in succession, the top object on the stack resolves [405.5]. Counterspell is on top of the stack, so it resolves before Divination. Counterspell's effect counters target spell (Divination). Countering a spell means canceling it and removing it from the stack; it doesn't resolve and none of its effects occur [701.6a]. Therefore, Divination never resolves and goes to the graveyard. After Counterspell finishes resolving, it too is put into its owner's graveyard as the final part of its resolution [608.2n], leaving the stack empty.

results.question: My [Charging Rhino] has trample and is blocked by [Vampire Nighthawk], which has deathtouch. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to the player?
results.text:
You must assign at least 3 damage to Vampire Nighthawk before you can trample any excess damage to the defending player.

Trample (rule 702.19b) requires you to assign lethal damage to all blocking creatures before assigning excess damage to the player or planeswalker being attacked. Lethal damage is normally an amount equal to the creature's toughness minus any damage already marked on it (rule 302.4b). Vampire Nighthawk is a 2/3, so its toughness is 3, and with no prior damage marked, lethal damage is 3.

The deathtouch ability on Vampire Nighthawk does not change this. Rule 702.2c says that any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered lethal for excess damage purposes. That rule applies only when the source dealing the damage has deathtouch. Here, the attacking Charging Rhino does not have deathtouch, so the standard toughness-based lethal damage applies. Therefore, Charging Rhino must assign 3 damage to Vampire Nighthawk, and the remaining 1 damage (since Charging Rhino is a 4/4) can be assigned to the defending player via trample.

results.question: I have [Monastery Swiftspear] on the battlefield and I cast [Shardless Agent]. When its cascade ability puts a noncreature spell onto the stack, does Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger before or after that cascaded spell resolves?
results.text:
Monastery Swiftspear's prowess triggers when you cast the cascaded spell, and that trigger goes on the stack above that spell, so it resolves before the cascaded spell does.

Here's why: When you cast Shardless Agent, its cascade ability triggers and goes on the stack above Shardless Agent. Cascade resolves, and during its resolution you may cast the exiled noncreature spell without paying its mana cost. Casting that spell causes Monastery Swiftspear's prowess to trigger (rule 702.108a). According to rule 601.2i, abilities that trigger when a spell is cast trigger at that moment, but they aren't put onto the stack until a player would receive priority. Since cascade is still resolving, no player gets priority yet. After cascade finishes resolving, the active player gets priority, and before that, any triggered abilities that have triggered are put onto the stack. Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger is placed on top of the cascaded spell (as confirmed by Monastery Swiftspear ruling #2: "Prowess goes on the stack on top of the spell that caused it to trigger. It will resolve before that spell."). The cascaded spell is already on the stack above Shardless Agent (Shardless Agent ruling #1). Thus, when players pass priority, the prowess trigger resolves first, giving Monastery Swiftspear +1/+1 until end of turn, and only then does the cascaded spell resolve.

results.question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?
results.text: Yes, state-based actions will destroy the Grizzly Bears before Lightning Bolt resolves. The Grizzly Bears has 2 damage marked on it, which equals its toughness of 2, so it has been dealt lethal damage [120.6]. State-based actions are checked each time a player would receive priority [117.5], and before a spell resolves, all players must pass priority in succession [608.1]. Therefore, before Lightning Bolt resolves, the game checks state-based actions, sees the lethal damage on Grizzly Bears, and destroys it. This happens automatically and does not use the stack.

results.question: It's my upkeep. My [Phyrexian Arena]'s beginning-of-upkeep trigger and my opponent's own beginning-of-upkeep trigger both want to go on the stack. Who chooses the order, and when exactly do they trigger?
results.text:
Both triggers go on the stack at the beginning of your upkeep step, before any player gets priority. You, as the active player, put your Phyrexian Arena trigger on the stack first, then the opponent puts their trigger on the stack. This means the opponent's trigger resolves first.

This answer assumes the opponent's trigger is one that triggers at the beginning of your upkeep (for example, "At the beginning of each opponent's upkeep, ..."). If the opponent's trigger instead triggers only at the beginning of their own upkeep, it would not trigger during your upkeep at all, and only your Phyrexian Arena trigger would go on the stack.

**When they trigger:** According to rule 500.6, when a step begins, any abilities that trigger "at the beginning of" that step trigger immediately. The upkeep step has no turn-based actions (503.1a), so these triggers are the first thing to happen after the step begins. They trigger simultaneously.

**Order on the stack:** After triggering, they are put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority (117.3a, 603.3b). Since multiple abilities triggered, rule 603.3b applies: first, each player in APNAP order (Active Player, then Non-Active Player) puts their triggered abilities with a trigger condition that isn't another ability triggering on the stack in any order they choose. Here, both triggers are from the step beginning, not from another ability triggering. You are the active player, so you put your Phyrexian Arena trigger on the stack first. Then the opponent puts their trigger on the stack on top of yours. The stack resolves from the top down, so the opponent's trigger resolves first.

results.question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
results.text:
Exactly one card ends up back in your hand: the original sorcery card you cast. The copy created by Fork does not return a card to your hand.

When the original sorcery resolves, its buyback replacement effect applies because you paid the buyback cost. Rule 702.27a says that if the buyback cost was paid, the spell is put into its owner's hand instead of the graveyard as it resolves. So that physical card goes to your hand.

The copy made by Fork is not a card (rule 707.10). Fork ruling #8 explicitly states: "If you copy a spell for which Buyback has been paid, you get nothing back since the copied spell does not have a card to give you." The copy's buyback replacement effect would try to put a card into your hand, but there is no card associated with the copy, so nothing happens. The copy simply ceases to exist after it resolves (or would go to the graveyard, but as a non-card it can't).

Therefore, only the original sorcery card returns to your hand.

results.question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
results.text: No, you do not get a token. Mimic Vat's ruling #0 directly covers this situation: if the exiled card is a nonpermanent card (such as an instant or sorcery that was manifested), no token is created. Lightning Bolt is an instant, so when Mimic Vat's activated ability resolves, it attempts to create a token copy of a nonpermanent card and fails to produce a token.

results.question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
results.text:
Yes, both exiled creatures return to the battlefield under their owners' control when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield.

Fiend Hunter has two linked abilities: the enters-the-battlefield ability that exiles a creature, and the leaves-the-battlefield ability that returns "the exiled card." When you copy the enters-the-battlefield ability with Lithoform Engine, the copy is also linked to the leaves-the-battlefield ability. As stated in Lithoform Engine's rulings, "If an ability is linked to a second ability, copies of that first ability are also linked to that second ability. If the second ability refers to 'the exiled card,' it refers to all cards exiled by the first ability and the copy." Therefore, when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield, its leaves-the-battlefield ability returns both creatures exiled by the original ability and the copy.

results.question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
results.text: No, the exiled creature does not return to the battlefield. Phasing out does not cause a permanent to leave the battlefield (rule 702.26d), so Banishing Light's "until this enchantment leaves the battlefield" condition is not met. Teferi's Protection ruling #21 explicitly confirms that one-shot effects waiting for a permanent to leave the battlefield, like Banishing Light's, won't happen when that permanent phases out. The creature remains exiled.

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
results.text: Yes, Counterspell can target Emrakul, the Promised End while it's on the stack. Protection from instants only functions while Emrakul is on the battlefield, not while it's a spell on the stack. If Counterspell resolves and counters Emrakul, the cast trigger ("When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent...") is a separate triggered ability that already went on the stack above Emrakul. It will still resolve normally, so you will control that opponent's next turn even though Emrakul itself was countered.

results.question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
results.text:
Yes, Valki, God of Lies is a legal cascade hit if the cascade spell's mana value is 3 or greater, because the exiled double-faced card's mana value is that of its front face (Valki, God of Lies), which is 2. You can cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor side for free only if the cascade spell's mana value is 8 or greater; otherwise, the resulting spell's mana value of 7 is not less than the cascade spell's mana value, so you may not cast it without paying its mana cost. If the cascade spell's mana value is 2 or less, Valki, God of Lies is not a legal hit at all.

Cascade (rule 702.85a) exiles cards until you exile a nonland card with mana value less than the cascade spell's mana value. While in exile, a double-faced card has only the characteristics of its front face by default (implied by rules 712.11c and 712.14b, which establish the front face as the default for casting and entering the battlefield). Therefore, the exiled Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor has mana value 2. If that is less than the cascade spell's mana value, it stops the exile process. Then cascade allows you to cast that card without paying its mana cost, but only if the resulting spell's mana value is also less than the cascade spell's mana value. Because Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor is a modal double-faced card, you may cast either face that fits the criteria (ruling #16). If you choose Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor, the resulting spell has mana value 7, so it can be cast for free only when the cascade spell's mana value is 8 or more. If you choose Valki, God of Lies, its mana value 2 must be less than the cascade spell's mana value (i.e., cascade spell's mana value 3 or more). If the cascade spell's mana value is exactly 2, neither face qualifies because the exiled card's mana value is not less than 2, and even if it were, the resulting spell's mana value would not be less than 2.
citations: Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
results.text:
You control exactly one of the opponent's turns (their next turn), you get a second Emrakul as a token, and copying the Emrakul spell does **not** give you another control-a-turn trigger.

Here's the breakdown, assuming both copies of the triggered ability target the same opponent:

1. **Copying the cast trigger** – You activate Lithoform Engine's first ability targeting the Emrakul cast trigger on the stack. This creates a copy of that triggered ability (rule 707.10; Lithoform Engine ruling #3). The copy resolves and sets up its own "gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn" and "after that turn, that player takes an extra turn" effect. The original trigger then resolves and does the same.

2. **Overwriting control effects** – When multiple player-controlling effects affect the same player, the last one created overwrites the others (Emrakul ruling #14). The copy that resolved last (the one put on the stack later) will control the opponent's next turn; the earlier effect's control is overwritten. However, **both** effects still create an extra turn (Emrakul ruling #14). Those extra turns are both scheduled after the opponent's next turn (the one you control). The most recently created extra turn is taken first (rule 500.7). So the opponent's next turn is controlled by you, then they take two extra turns in a row (the order depends on which trigger resolved last).

3. **Copying the permanent spell** – After untapping Lithoform Engine with Voltaic Key, you activate Lithoform Engine's third ability targeting the Emrakul spell on the stack. This puts a copy of the permanent spell onto the stack (rule 707.10; Lithoform Engine ruling #5). The copy is not cast, so no "when you cast" ability triggers (Lithoform Engine ruling #6). When the copy resolves, it becomes a token copy of Emrakul, the Promised End (rule 111.13). You now have the original Emrakul spell (which will also resolve into a creature) and a token Emrakul.

Thus, you control one opponent turn, you get a second Emrakul (a token), and copying the spell yields no extra control trigger.

results.question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
results.text:
Yes, you get two tokens. When you copy Mimic Vat’s activated ability with Lithoform Engine, the copy is put on the stack and resolves, creating a token that’s a copy of the card exiled with Mimic Vat. Then the original ability resolves and creates another token. Both tokens will have haste and be exiled at the beginning of the next end step.

Lithoform Engine’s first ability creates a copy of the activated ability on the stack. According to [707.10b], a copy of an ability has the same source as the original ability, so the copy refers to the same Mimic Vat artifact. Mimic Vat’s activated ability says “Create a token that’s a copy of a card exiled with this artifact.” Because there is a card exiled with Mimic Vat (you imprinted a creature), both the original and the copy will see that exiled card and create a token copy of it. Rule [607.3] covers linked abilities that refer to “a card” exiled with the object; with only one exiled card, both abilities simply use that card. Rule [111.12] and Mimic Vat ruling #6 confirm that a token is created as long as a card is exiled with Mimic Vat when the ability resolves. Lithoform Engine ruling #0 also confirms the copy’s source is the same as the original’s.

results.question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
results.text:
If you cast Awaken the Woods with X=0, the total cost is {1}{G}{G} (three mana) and you create zero tokens. For the best value, you should choose X=2, which also costs {1}{G}{G} but gives you two 1/1 tokens.

Here's why: Awaken the Woods has mana cost {X}{G}{G}. You choose X as you cast it (rule 107.3a). Your cost reducer lowers the generic portion of the total cost by {1}. Trinisphere's effect applies last, after all cost increases and reductions, and sets the mana component to three if it would be less than three (Trinisphere ruling #0).

- With X=0, the mana cost is {G}{G}. After the {1} reduction (which can't reduce colored mana), the cost is still {G}{G} (two mana). Trinisphere sees a mana component of two, so it raises the cost to three mana: you pay {1}{G}{G} and get zero tokens.
- With X=1, the mana cost is {1}{G}{G}. After reduction, it's {G}{G} (two mana). Trinisphere again bumps it to three mana: you pay {1}{G}{G} for one token.
- With X=2, the mana cost is {2}{G}{G}. After reduction, it's {1}{G}{G} (three mana). Trinisphere sees three mana and does nothing. You pay {1}{G}{G} for two tokens.
- With X=3, the cost becomes {2}{G}{G} (four mana) for three tokens, and so on.

Thus X=2 gives you the most tokens per mana spent (two tokens for three mana).

results.question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
results.text:
Yes, you can target Grist, the Hunger Tide with Animate Dead because Grist is a creature card in your graveyard. However, Grist will end up back in your graveyard.

Here's what happens step by step:
1. You cast Animate Dead targeting Grist, the Hunger Tide in your graveyard. Grist is a legal target because its static ability makes it a 1/1 Insect creature card while it's not on the battlefield.
2. Animate Dead enters the battlefield attached to Grist in the graveyard.
3. Animate Dead's enters-the-battlefield triggered ability goes on the stack. When it resolves, it returns Grist to the battlefield under your control and tries to attach Animate Dead to it.
4. On the battlefield, Grist is no longer a creature (its static ability only applies when it's not on the battlefield). Animate Dead's new enchant ability says "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura." Since Grist is not a creature, Animate Dead can't legally enchant it.
5. State-based actions are checked. Animate Dead is an Aura attached to an illegal permanent, so it's put into its owner's graveyard.
6. Animate Dead leaving the battlefield triggers its own delayed triggered ability: "When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it." That trigger goes on the stack.
7. When the sacrifice trigger resolves, you sacrifice Grist, the Hunger Tide. Grist goes back to the graveyard.

This outcome is directly covered by Animate Dead's ruling #4: if the returned creature can't legally be enchanted by Animate Dead, the Aura goes to the graveyard and the delayed trigger will force a sacrifice.
citations: Grist, the Hunger Tide static ability

results.question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
results.text:
Yes, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave keeps its four +1/+1 counters when it dies and you move it to the command zone, and it enters the battlefield with those counters when you recast it. Doubling Season does **not** double those counters.

Skullbriar's own ability says "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." This overrides the general rule [122.2] that counters cease to exist when an object changes zones. The command zone is not a hand or library, so the counters stay on Skullbriar when you apply the commander state-based action [704.6d] to move it from the graveyard to the command zone [903.9b]. The counters also remain on Skullbriar as it moves from the command zone to the stack and then to the battlefield during the casting process, because none of those zones are a hand or library. Therefore, Skullbriar enters the battlefield already carrying the four +1/+1 counters.

Doubling Season's replacement effect only applies when an effect would put counters on a permanent you control. The counters on Skullbriar are not being put on by an effect; they are simply retained due to Skullbriar's own static ability. As stated in Skullbriar's ruling #2, "The counters that remain on Skullbriar as it changes zones aren't 'placed' on Skullbriar. Effects like Doubling Season's ... won't affect those counters." So Doubling Season does not double them.

results.question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
results.text:
No, you do not lose the game during that extra turn. However, the "lose the game" ability from Final Fortune does not simply vanish—it will trigger at the beginning of the next turn's end step instead, so you will lose the game at that time unless you can prevent it.

When you activate Sundial of the Infinite before the end step, the turn ends immediately and the end step is skipped. Rule [724.1e] states that "at the beginning of the end step" triggered abilities don't trigger because the end step is skipped. Sundial of the Infinite's ruling #1 clarifies that such abilities will trigger at the beginning of the end step of the next turn. Therefore, Final Fortune's delayed trigger waits for the next end step that actually occurs, and you will lose the game when that trigger resolves unless you intervene.

Note that Final Fortune ruling #1 ("If you end up skipping the extra turn that is gained, you do not lose the game") does not apply here because you are not skipping the extra turn—you are taking it and ending it early. The trigger is merely postponed, not avoided entirely.

results.question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
results.text:
You choose what Clone copies as it enters the battlefield, during the resolution of the Clone spell. The choice is made by you (Clone's controller) without using the stack, and your opponent cannot respond to that choice directly. They can only respond to the Clone spell while it's on the stack, before it resolves and you make the choice.

Clone's ability is a replacement effect that modifies how it enters the battlefield. Rule 707.5 states that an object that enters "as a copy" becomes a copy as it enters, not after. Rule 707.6 clarifies that when a permanent enters as a copy, its controller makes any "as [this] enters" choices—in this case, choosing which creature to copy. Clone's ability doesn't target (Clone ruling #0), so you simply choose any creature already on the battlefield (Clone ruling #2). Because this happens during the resolution of the spell, no player gets priority until after Clone has entered and the choice is made. Thus, your opponent can't respond to the choice itself; they can only cast spells or activate abilities in response to the Clone spell before it resolves.

results.question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
results.text:
You get three lands total. The original Flooded Strand ability and the two copies created by Gogo, Master of Mimicry will each resolve, letting you search for a Plains or Island and put it onto the battlefield.

Here's why: When you activate Flooded Strand's ability, you pay its costs (tap, pay 1 life, sacrifice it) and put the ability on the stack. Then you activate Gogo's ability with X=2, targeting that ability on the stack. Gogo's ability resolves and creates two copies of the targeted ability on the stack (rule 707.10b, Gogo ruling #6). The copies have the same source as the original (Gogo ruling #9) and are independent of the original permanent's presence. The original ability remains on the stack below the copies. All three abilities resolve in order (the copies first, then the original), and each one instructs you to search your library for a Plains or Island card and put it onto the battlefield. Since the ability doesn't require the source to still be on the battlefield, you get a land from each resolution.
